title: Against, Around, Backward, Before
theme: Prefixes contra-/counter-, circum-, retro- and pre-
objectives: I can use the prefixes contra-/counter- (against), circum- (around), retro- (backward), and pre- (before) to work out hard words.
I can sort ten words by the direction their prefix points: against, around, backward, or before.
I can explain what it means to circumvent a rule and why a rule can fail even when it sounds fair.
I can write a short reflection using retrospect and at least three other words from this unit.
rationale: Four prefixes of opposition, circling, reversal and time give students a reading tool for hard words they will meet in law, history and science. The set is built so the direction of each prefix can be checked against the word: against (contraband, counteract, contrary), around (circumvent, circumstance), backward (retroactive, retrospect) and before (preclude, premature, predecessor). Several words are most useful in discussions of rules and decisions, so they connect to the objection and rebuttal work in the rhetoric units and to the ethics units earlier in the year. The passage, a student council story, uses nearly every word in a setting about how and why a rule fails.

words.def: Goods that it is illegal or forbidden to bring in, sell, or have.
words.ex: Customs officers found contraband hidden under a false floor in the truck.
words.ex2: At the school dance, chaperones collected any contraband, such as fireworks, at the door.
words.nonExample: A sandwich in your lunch bag is not contraband, since no rule forbids it.

morph.note: Goods that go against a ban.

apps.academic: Customs laws define contraband and give officers the power to seize it.
apps.spoken: Phones are contraband during the test, so put them in the box.
apps.writing: Name what makes an item contraband, which is the rule or law that forbids it.

cloze.s: The border officer opened the crate and found ___ hidden among the oranges.

cloze2.s: Phones are treated as ___ in the exam room, so students must leave them in the bin.

misuse.s: The inspector praised the shipment of contraband because it was fully legal and properly labeled.
misuse.why: Contraband is forbidden or illegal; a legal, properly labeled shipment is not.

visual.alt: A sealed crate with a red prohibition sign.

words.def: To reduce or cancel the effect of something by acting against it.
words.ex: A cold compress can counteract the swelling from a bump.
words.ex2: The city counteracted the spread of rumors by posting accurate information every hour.
words.nonExample: Pouring more water into a flooded basement does not counteract the flood.

apps.academic: An antidote is a substance that counteracts the effect of a poison.
apps.spoken: Exercise can counteract the stiffness from sitting all day.
apps.writing: Say what counteracts what, such as a medicine, a policy, or an action working against an effect.

cloze.s: Drinking plenty of water can help ___ the effects of a hot afternoon in the sun.

cloze2.s: The coach added speed drills to ___ the heavy, slow style that the team had picked up.

misuse.s: To counteract the fire, the crew poured gasoline on it so that it would burn even hotter.
misuse.why: To counteract is to cancel an effect; adding gasoline strengthens the fire instead.

visual.alt: A balance scale with arrows pushing in opposite directions.

words.def: Opposite or very different; going against something else.
words.ex: Contrary to what the forecast predicted, the afternoon turned sunny.
words.ex2: Their opinions were contrary, so the debate went on for an hour.
words.nonExample: Two friends who agree on every point do not hold contrary views.

morph.note: The final a of contra- is dropped before -ary (contra -> contr).

apps.academic: Scientists revise a theory when new evidence is contrary to its predictions.
apps.spoken: Contrary to popular belief, bats are not blind.
apps.writing: Use contrary to to introduce evidence that goes against what people expected.

cloze.s: The test results were ___ to the doctor's expectation, showing improvement where she had feared decline.

cloze2.s: Maya's plan was ___ to her brother's, so the two of them argued over the map all the way to the lake.

misuse.s: The two reports were contrary, because both said exactly the same thing in the same words.
misuse.why: Contrary means opposite or in conflict; two reports that match exactly are not.

visual.alt: Two arrows that point in opposite directions.

words.def: To find a way around a rule, obstacle, or problem, especially by clever or sneaky means.
words.ex: Some drivers circumvent the traffic jam by taking narrow side streets.
words.ex2: The company tried to circumvent the law by shipping its waste through another country.
words.nonExample: Obeying a rule openly is not circumventing it.

apps.academic: Lawyers study how companies circumvent regulations and how laws can be written to close the loopholes.
apps.spoken: He tried to circumvent the filter by changing a few letters.
apps.writing: Circumvent suggests avoiding a rule instead of breaking it head-on, so say what is being avoided.

cloze.s: Rather than wait in the long line, some students tried to ___ it by sneaking in through the side door.

cloze2.s: The company hired lawyers to ___ the new safety rules without technically breaking them.

misuse.s: She circumvented the rule by following it carefully and doing exactly what it said.
misuse.why: To circumvent is to get around a rule; following it exactly is the opposite.

visual.alt: A curved arrow that goes around a construction barrier.

words.frame: People might circumvent a rule by ___.

words.def: A condition or fact connected with an event or situation.
words.ex: A single unexpected circumstance, a broken bridge, changed the whole route of the race.
words.ex2: Under the circumstances, the school decided to cancel the picnic.
words.nonExample: Your favorite color is not a circumstance of the traffic accident, because it has no connection to the event.

morph.note: Literally the things that stand around an event.

apps.academic: Historians explain events by looking at the circumstances in which people made their choices.
apps.spoken: Under no circumstances should you open that door.
apps.writing: Use circumstances to name the conditions around an event, and explain why they matter.

cloze.s: A single ___, such as a missed bus, can change the whole shape of a student's day.

cloze2.s: Given the ___ of the storm, the school allowed students to arrive an hour late.

misuse.s: The circumstances of the accident were that nothing had happened and nobody was there.
misuse.why: Circumstances are the conditions around an event; a statement that nothing happened names none.

visual.alt: Rain clouds above a road barrier.

words.def: Taking effect from an earlier date, so that it applies to things that already happened.
words.ex: The raise was retroactive to January, so workers received extra pay for the months already past.
words.ex2: The league made the new rule retroactive, so last season's scores were recalculated under it.
words.nonExample: A rule that starts next Monday and applies only to the future is not retroactive.

apps.academic: A retroactive law applies to actions that happened before it was passed, and the United States Constitution forbids retroactive criminal laws.
apps.spoken: The discount was retroactive, so I got money back on last week's order.
apps.writing: Say the date that a retroactive change reaches back to.

cloze.s: The company announced a ___ pay raise that covered the three months employees had already worked.

cloze2.s: Because the new rule was ___, scores from last month's contest were recalculated under it.

misuse.s: A retroactive law applies only to events that have not happened yet.
misuse.why: Retroactive means reaching back to earlier events; applying only to the future is the opposite.

visual.alt: A rewind symbol beside a calendar.

words.def: A look back at past events, especially to understand them better.
words.ex: In retrospect, the team realized that the loud practice the night before had tired them out.
words.ex2: With the clarity of retrospect, the coach saw that the trade had been a mistake.
words.nonExample: A prediction about next year is foresight, not retrospect.

apps.academic: Historians view events in retrospect, knowing what happened next, which people at the time could not know.
apps.spoken: In retrospect, I should have started studying earlier.
apps.writing: In retrospect is a handy opening for a reflective sentence: name the choice, then the lesson.

cloze.s: In ___, the explorers admitted that they should have packed more food for the journey.

cloze2.s: Seen in ___, the quiet before the storm was a warning that nobody had noticed.

misuse.s: In retrospect, I predict exactly what will happen to the team next season.
misuse.why: Retrospect is looking back at the past; predicting next season looks forward.

visual.alt: A back arrow beside a pair of eyes.

words.def: To prevent something from happening or to make it impossible.
words.ex: A broken leg would preclude her from running in the race.
words.ex2: The contract precludes either side from sharing the plans with a competitor.
words.nonExample: A rainy forecast does not preclude a picnic if you bring a tent.

apps.academic: A signed agreement may preclude a company from sharing its customers' information.
apps.spoken: Her schedule precludes any trips this month.
apps.writing: Preclude is formal and strong; it means that something has become impossible, not just difficult.

cloze.s: The strict deadline will ___ anyone from handing in the project late, because the website closes at midnight.

cloze2.s: A serious knee injury can ___ an athlete from competing for an entire season.

misuse.s: The lock on the gate precluded the hikers from entering, so they walked right in.
misuse.why: To preclude is to prevent; if the hikers simply walked in, the lock prevented nothing.

visual.alt: A road barrier with a padlock hanging on it.

words.frame: A broken ___ would preclude me from ___.

words.def: Happening, done, or ready too soon; before the proper time.
words.ex: It was premature to announce the winner before every vote had been counted.
words.ex2: The premature frost killed the tomato plants before they could ripen.
words.nonExample: A result announced after the last vote is counted is not premature.

apps.academic: Premature conclusions can result when scientists draw a result from too little data.
apps.spoken: Do not celebrate yet; it is premature.
apps.writing: Premature criticizes timing: it means before there is enough information or readiness.

cloze.s: The coach said it was ___ to name a starting lineup before the final tryout had even taken place.

cloze2.s: The ___ celebration ended awkwardly when the referee announced that the game was not over.

misuse.s: The bus was premature because it showed up ten minutes after its scheduled time.
misuse.why: Premature means too early; arriving ten minutes late is the opposite.

visual.alt: A green, unripe apple beside an alarm clock.

words.frame: It would be premature to ___ before ___.

words.def: A person or thing that came before another in a job, role, or sequence.
words.ex: The new principal kept many of the programs started by her predecessor.
words.ex2: The latest phone is faster than its predecessor, though the older model still works.
words.nonExample: The person who takes a job next is a successor, not a predecessor.

apps.academic: A good biography compares a leader with the predecessor who held the office before.
apps.spoken: My predecessor left me a note with instructions.
apps.writing: Pair predecessor with the role, as in the predecessor as mayor.

cloze.s: The new coach praised her ___ for building a strong team that she now had the chance to lead.

cloze2.s: The tablet is thinner than its ___, though the earlier model had a longer battery life.

misuse.s: The new mayor thanked her predecessor, who would take the job next year.
misuse.why: A predecessor came before; the person who comes after is a successor.

visual.alt: A key beside a handwritten note left for the next person.

passage.title: The Rule Nobody Could Enforce
paras: When Marisol became student council president, her predecessor had taped a note to the desk: “Good luck with the vending machine.” The previous council had banned energy drinks from campus, and by October the cans were being traded in lockers like contraband. Marisol's first job was to find out why a rule that sounded so simple had failed.

She learned that nearly every student had found a way to circumvent it. Some filled water bottles at home, and some kept cans in a friend's gym bag. “Under the circumstances,” the principal told her, “we cannot search every backpack.” Marisol agreed that checking everyone would be unfair and expensive. Her classmates' view, however, was contrary to the council's: they felt that the ban insulted them instead of protecting them.

Marisol did not want to scrap the rule in a hurry. A premature decision could leave students with less protection and no plan at all. So she asked the school nurse to explain how large amounts of caffeine can disturb sleep and raise a teenager's heart rate. The talk helped counteract some myths, such as the idea that the drinks provide free energy.

In the end the council wrote a new policy. High-caffeine drinks would not be sold in the cafeteria, but students would not be punished for carrying one from home, and an education campaign would replace the penalties. One student asked that the change be retroactive, so that detentions already given under the old rule would be erased. The council agreed. “A rule that precludes any chance to explain itself will not last,” Marisol said.

Years later, in retrospect, she would say that the lesson was bigger than a vending machine. A rule needs reasons that the people it governs can accept. She left a note of her own for the next president: “Explain before you ban.”

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word “contraband” most nearly means
choices: gifts that friends exchange
healthy snacks from home
items that a rule forbids
goods sold in the cafeteria
qs.why: The ban made the cans forbidden, and the students traded them secretly in lockers.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, to “circumvent” the rule means to
choices: get around it without confronting it directly
ask the principal to change it
follow it more carefully
write a new rule to replace it
qs.why: The students filled water bottles at home and hid cans in bags, which let them get around the ban without openly breaking it.

qs.q: Why does Marisol avoid making a premature decision about the ban?
choices: She plans to cancel the council meeting.
She believes the ban is working well.
The principal told her not to change anything.
She wants to understand the problem first so that students are not left with less protection and no plan.
qs.why: She says a hasty decision could leave students with less protection and no plan, so she consults the nurse and holds a hearing before changing the rule.

qs.q: Which detail shows that the new policy was made retroactive?
choices: The education campaign began the next semester.
Detentions already given under the old rule were erased.
The cafeteria stopped selling high-caffeine drinks.
Students could carry a drink from home.
qs.why: A retroactive change reaches back to earlier events, and the council erased penalties given before the new policy.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Students should never be allowed to drink anything with caffeine.
A principal should search backpacks whenever a rule is broken.
Rules work best when the people they affect understand and accept the reasons for them.
Student councils should have no power to change rules.
qs.why: The ban failed because students saw no reason to accept it, and Marisol's final note, Explain before you ban, sums up the lesson.

write.prompt: Think of a rule at school or at home that people often find ways to get around. Use at least three words from this unit to explain why the rule fails and how it could be improved.
write.frame: In retrospect, the rule failed because ___. A better rule would ___, which would ___.

study.task: Sort the ten unit words by the direction their prefix points: against, around, backward, or before. For each word, write the prefix, say what it adds, and check that the direction fits the meaning. Then choose the word where the prefix hint is least helpful and explain why.

Write a sentence that uses premature to describe a decision made too early, and say what should have happened first.

given: The rule was announced on Monday.
It applied to detentions from last month.
combine.model: Because the rule announced on Monday was retroactive and applied to last month's detentions, students were relieved.
The nurse's talk helped counteract some myths, and students rethought the ban.

discuss: Is it ever right to circumvent a rule? Use circumvent and one other word from the unit.
Why might a rule that is retroactive be unfair? Why might it be fair?
How do circumstances change whether a decision is premature?
produce.explain: Explain how knowing the prefix retro- helps you understand both retroactive and retrospect.

argue.prompt: Claim: Schools should explain the reasons for a new rule before enforcing it. Take a side and support it with two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. Without an explanation, students may ___, but with one, they ___.

constructed.prompt: A school bans phones during tests. Explain what makes a phone contraband in that room and how a student might try to circumvent the rule. Use both words.
look: describes a realistic way to get around the rule
constructed.model: A phone is contraband during a test because the rule forbids it. A student might circumvent the rule by hiding a phone in a sleeve instead of leaving it in the bin.

constructed.prompt: Describe a decision that turned out to be premature and what you learned in retrospect. Use both words.
look: describes a decision made too early
states a clear lesson learned from looking back
constructed.model: I made a premature decision to sign up for three clubs before I saw how much homework I had. In retrospect, I should have joined one and waited a month before adding another.

constructed.prompt: A new coach takes over a team from her predecessor. Explain one circumstance that might make her job harder or easier. Use both words.
look: connects it to the new coach's task
constructed.model: One circumstance that might make her job easier is that her predecessor built strong practice habits. The new coach can keep them and add her own ideas.

teacher.overview: Students use four families of prefixes (contra-/counter-, circum-, retro-, pre-) to read ten words that appear in law, history, science and literature, and then use the words to discuss why rules fail. The prefix direction (against, around, backward, before) is the organizing idea, and every word can be checked against it. The narrative about a student council ties the words to rules, decisions and consequences.

notes.va.contraband.n: Contraband is goods that rules or laws forbid. The prefix contra- (against) helps with meaning. Ask what makes an item contraband in different places: an airport, an exam room, a border. Students may think contraband always means dangerous; it can mean any forbidden item.
notes.va.counteract.v: Counteract is counter- (against) plus act. Use a balance picture: something works against an effect. Students sometimes use it to mean simply stop; ask whether the effect is reduced or canceled. Compare with prevent.
notes.va.contrary.adj: Contrary has the pattern contra- plus -ary, with a dropped a. Teach the phrase contrary to, which is very common in news and science writing. Be aware that contrary also has an everyday meaning of stubborn, which is not taught here.
notes.va.circumvent.v: Circumvent means to get around a rule or obstacle. It carries a note of cleverness or sneakiness. The prefix circum- (around) helps with meaning even though the rest of the word is not broken down here. Ask students whether circumventing a rule is the same as breaking it.
notes.va.circumstance.n: Circumstance is circum- (around) plus stance, the way something stands: the conditions around an event. Most students meet the plural, circumstances. Practice the phrases under the circumstances and under no circumstances.
notes.va.retroactive.adj: Retroactive is retro- (backward) plus act plus -ive. Ask for examples: a pay raise that reaches back, a rule that applies to past events. A retroactive law is a legal concept; the United States Constitution forbids retroactive criminal laws, which you can mention for advanced students.
notes.va.retrospect.n: Retrospect is retro- (backward) plus spect (look): a looking back. The phrase in retrospect is the common use. Students enjoy writing a sentence that begins with it. Contrast with foresight and hindsight.
notes.va.preclude.v: Preclude is formal and means to make impossible. The prefix pre- (before) hints at acting in advance. Students may confuse it with include; show the contrast. Ask for something that precludes sleeping at night.
notes.va.premature.adj: Premature is pre- (before) plus mature: before it is ready. Students know premature from news about babies and from phrases such as premature celebration. Ask what has to happen for a decision to stop being premature.
notes.va.predecessor.n: Predecessor is pre- (before) plus de- plus cess plus -or. The pieces together suggest one who went away before. The opposite is successor. Have students name predecessors and successors in school roles, sports and history.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The word circumvent starts with circum-, around, and the students find ways around the ban. A premature decision has pre-, before, so it is too early. Retroactive has retro-, backward, so it reaches back to earlier events. In retrospect has the same retro-, and it means looking back.”
discuss: Can a rule be fair and still fail? What makes people circumvent rules?
What would you want to know before making a decision that might be premature?
Why do historians value retrospect, and what can it miss?
misconceptions: Circumvent means to break a rule openly.
Predecessor and successor mean the same thing.
extend: Collect five words that begin with these prefixes from your reading and sort them by direction.
Write a short scene in which a new club president meets a problem left by a predecessor.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Bring back rebuttal, objection, paradox and irony when students discuss the council's rule and the students' reaction. Revisit circumvent and preclude after two days with a new rule, and return to retro- and pre- when students meet retrofit, prefix or prejudge.

wida.oral: Partner A names one of the four prefixes. Partner B names a unit word with that prefix and says what the prefix tells them about the word.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: contrabando, contrarrestar, contrario, eludir/sortear (circumvent), circunstancia, retroactivo, retrospectiva/mirada atrás, impedir/excluir (preclude), prematuro, predecesor.

Morphology: contraband is segmented as contra- plus band (a ban or official order); this reflects the usual account but should be confirmed with an etymology source. Circumvent, preclude and the second element of predecessor are not fully segmented because the final pieces (vent, clude) are not in the morphology dataset.
The note that the United States Constitution forbids retroactive criminal laws (ex post facto) should be confirmed before publication.
Fact claims in the passage: caffeine can disturb sleep and raise heart rate (general statement; the passage is fictional).
Teacher note for contrary mentions the everyday sense of stubborn (not taught).
